# KV Cache: A Technical Overview

## What Is KV Cache?

In transformer-based language models, inference requires computing token representations at every forward pass. During autoregressive generation, each new token depends on all previously generated tokens. The Key-Value (KV) cache is an optimization that stores the computed keys and values from attention computations so they don't need to be recalculated for every new token.

When processing a sequence, the model computes query (Q), key (K), and value (V) matrices for each token. For token generation beyond the first, only the current token produces a new query, while all prior tokens' keys and values remain unchanged. Without caching, the system would recompute K and V for the entire context length at each step—a quadratic cost in sequence length. With KV caching, each step incurs only linear compute relative to the single new token's projections plus the attention operation itself.

## Why It Matters for Long Context

Long context inference exposes fundamental scaling challenges in transformers. Consider generating 1,000 tokens with a 128,000-token context window: without caching, each step processes all 128,000 tokens twice (once for K, once for V), resulting in approximately 256 million operations per token—prohibitively expensive. KV caching reduces this to roughly 128,000 operations per token, a 2,000× improvement.

Beyond raw performance, KV caching enables practical applications that require extended context. Document summarization across lengthy inputs, multi-turn conversations spanning thousands of messages, code repositories analyzed as cohesive units, and retrieval-augmented generation over extensive knowledge bases all depend on efficient long-context handling. The cache transforms these use cases from theoretical possibilities into deployable systems.
